insight.title: Kubernetes controllers: reconcile desired state, do not script the happy path
insight.one_liner: A Kubernetes controller is a continuing reconciliation loop: observe current state, compare it with declared desired state, make or request a change, then observe again.
insight.why_this_matters: The controller model is a compact way to understand resilient automation under constant change. It replaces one-shot procedural assumptions with repeated convergence toward a declared target, while keeping each controller focused on a bounded responsibility.

whole_source_map.problem: A distributed system is continuously changing: resources fail, external systems drift, and one successful command does not guarantee that the intended state remains true.
whole_source_map.thesis: Represent desired state declaratively and use independent control loops that repeatedly observe current state and act to move it closer to the desired state.
core_topics: small focused controllers instead of one monolithic control loop
continuous convergence rather than stable completion

derived_model.problem: A one-shot automation can succeed once and still leave the system wrong later when reality changes.
derived_model.mechanism: A controller watches a resource whose spec expresses desired state, observes relevant current state, makes or requests bounded changes, reports state back, and repeats the loop.
derived_model.result: Automation becomes convergence-oriented: failures or drift can be corrected by later iterations without requiring one perfect end-to-end execution path.

central_chain: The API object expresses a desired state while the real system has a current state that may differ.
A controller repeatedly observes the relevant state rather than assuming one command permanently solved the problem.
When it detects a difference, it makes or requests a bounded change through the API server or an external system.
The changed state is observed again, so reconciliation continues as the environment changes.
Kubernetes composes many focused controllers, reducing the need for one tightly coupled monolithic control loop.
open_gaps: The conceptual page explains the controller pattern but not implementation-level controller-runtime mechanics such as work queues, rate limiting or generation handling.
The page does not claim that every controller action is automatically idempotent; safe repeated reconciliation still depends on controller and external-system design.

dominant.title: Reconciliation is a loop, not a one-time workflow

nodes.label: 01 · Declare
nodes.title: Desired state
nodes.text: A resource spec states what should be true.

nodes.label: 02 · Observe
nodes.title: Current state
nodes.text: The controller inspects what is actually true now.

nodes.label: 03 · Compare
nodes.title: Find the delta
nodes.text: The controller determines whether reality is close enough to the desired state.

nodes.label: 04 · Act
nodes.title: Make a bounded change
nodes.text: The controller changes an API object or an external system to reduce the delta.

nodes.label: 05 · Repeat
nodes.title: Observe again
nodes.text: The loop continues because the system can change again after any successful action.

concepts.name: Reconciliation loop
concepts.why_needed: The controller is defined by repeated observation and convergence, not by executing a fixed sequence once.

concepts.name: Desired state
concepts.why_needed: The resource spec gives the controller a declarative target that is separate from the current state of the world.

concepts.name: Current state
concepts.why_needed: Controllers need feedback about reality; desired state alone cannot tell whether corrective work is needed.

concepts.name: Focused controller responsibility
concepts.why_needed: Kubernetes prefers many controllers managing particular aspects of state rather than one interlinked monolithic control loop.

tool_map.name: Kubernetes API server
tool_map.why_explore: Built-in controllers commonly observe resources and request changes through the API server instead of directly performing every downstream action.
tool_map.relationship: Source-native Kubernetes component used by the controller pattern.

examples.scenario: A Job object declares that work should complete, while Pods are the resources that actually run the work.
examples.question: Can the Job controller keep creating or observing the required Pods until current state reflects the Job's desired outcome?

examples.scenario: A controller manages something outside the cluster such as node capacity.
examples.question: Can it observe desired state from the API, change the external system, and then report/observe the resulting state without assuming the first external call is final?

examples.scenario: A record should exist in several systems, but one downstream copy can disappear or lag after an earlier successful run.
examples.question: Would expressing the target state and periodically reconciling observed state be safer than treating the original workflow run as permanent proof of correctness?

limitations: Reconciliation does not remove the need for safe repeated side effects; a controller can still cause duplicates or oscillation if its actions are not designed for repetition.
Desired state can be wrong. A controller faithfully converging on a bad specification is still a failure.
Multiple controllers can interact through shared resources, so bounded responsibility reduces coupling but does not eliminate coordination problems.

The controller pattern is not the same as durable workflow execution: it focuses on continuously converging state, whereas a workflow engine may preserve the progress of a particular long-running execution.

use_now: When designing automation, distinguish a target condition that must remain true from a one-time sequence that merely attempted to create it.
For long-lived invariants, ask what observes drift after the original workflow finishes.
try: Model one operational invariant as desired state + observed state + reconciliation action instead of a procedural retry script.
build: A tiny reconciler that compares a declarative JSON target with observed state and emits only the corrective action required to close the delta.
watch: How controller-runtime implementations handle retries, backoff, event coalescing and stale observations.
ignore_for_now: Treating every business workflow as a Kubernetes-style controller; use reconciliation only where a persistent target state exists.

connections: durable execution: complementary but different — durable execution preserves progress of a workflow; reconciliation repeatedly converges a state invariant
controlled execution: a controller still needs authority and safe execution boundaries when corrective actions are consequential
idempotency under retry: repeated reconciliation makes duplicate-safe side effects an important implementation concern

concepts.label: Reconciliation loop
concepts.summary: A continuing control loop that observes current state, compares it with desired state and performs bounded corrective actions to reduce the difference.

concepts.label: Desired state
concepts.summary: A declarative representation of what a managed system or resource should look like, kept separate from observed reality.

concepts.label: Observed state
concepts.summary: The controller's current view of what is actually true, used as feedback for deciding whether corrective action is required.

relations.rationale: A controller needs an explicit target state in order to know what condition it should converge toward.
Reconciliation requires feedback about current reality so the controller can determine whether corrective work is necessary.
